t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we become acquainted with the introduction to the toxicological chemistry laboratory. The aim is to teach students the general condition, features and conditions of preliminary examination of objects submitted for toxicological chemical analysis. The plan consists of two parts. The first is an introduction to the toxicological chemistry module, objects and physical evidence. The second is the requirements for them. Within the topic, the determination of the purity of reagents used in forensic chemical practice is also considered.

There are four expected outcomes of the session. First, to know the types of objects and how to prepare them for analysis. Second, to determine the packaging and integrity of the submitted objects. Third, to examine the medium, colour and consistency of the physical evidence. Fourth, to master the identification of impurities that may occur in an object and their separate examination.

Let us consider the directions of toxicology. Toxicology studies the action of a poison on the body, that is toxicodynamics, and the transformation of a poison that has entered the body, that is toxicokinetics. At present there are three directions: theoretical, or experimental, preventive, or hygienic, and clinical. The theoretical direction studies the interaction of poison and organism, the preventive direction studies the degrees of hazard of substances and questions of protection from them, and the clinical direction studies chemical diseases. Toxicological chemistry is one of the main modules of the pharmaceutical profession; it teaches how to isolate poisons from an object and determine their quality and quantity.

t: The three sections of the module
n: The teaching of toxicological chemistry rests on three main sections. The first is forensic chemistry. It is considered the most fundamental and the most complex section of toxicological chemistry. The other two sections are: chemical determination of industrial and agricultural poisons in objects, and rapid express analysis of objects in acute poisoning. That is, the module consists of forensic chemistry, poisons of the national economy and express analysis.

Toxicological chemistry is linked with other sciences. Pharmacology and toxicology study the action of poisons on the organs of humans and animals. In determining the quality and quantity of poisons, methods of analytical and organic chemistry are applied. Toxicological and biological chemistry help in studying metabolites. Since poisoning is often caused by plants, the chemist must also know pharmacognosy.

Chemical-toxicological analysis has its own special features. Poisons belong to different chemical groups, and the objects examined are also varied. From a large quantity of biological material only a small, extremely small, quantity of poison is isolated. One works not with a pure substance but with isolates containing foreign substances. The poison changes in the body, so its metabolites are also determined. And finally, the forensic chemist is answerable to the judicial and investigative authorities.

The means required for the session: a textbook, lecture text, study aids, a funnel, test tubes, reagents, visual materials, adhesive tape and paper. As laboratory equipment, a room fitted with special laboratory facilities is needed. The object for the work: each student is given 100.0 g of liver and 25.0 ml of urine.

Rules of safety and preparation. The student brings to the laboratory work rubber gloves, a napkin and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed after work is finished. Objects from infectious persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are marked in the documents.

t: Methods of isolation, purification and determination
n: Methods of analysis are divided into two groups. The first is isolation of the substance from the object and purification. The second is determination of the quality and quantity of the isolated substance. As a result of isolation, the substance is brought into liquid form as a distillate, mineralisate or dialysate. For isolation, steam distillation, destruction, maceration with a solvent and dialysis are used; for purification, extraction and chromatography are used. Quality is determined by chemical and microcrystalloscopic methods, TLC, spectral characteristics and pharmacological action. Quantity is determined by acidimetry, alkalimetry, complexometric titration (trilonometry), photometry, spectrophotometry and GC.

t: Rooms of the forensic chemistry department
n: The rooms of the forensic chemistry department. The department in which forensic chemical examination analyses are carried out must have at least 5 rooms. In the first room objects are received and stored; there are a refrigerator and an iron safe there. The second is the laboratory in which investigations and examinations are carried out. In the third the sample is prepared and the external appearance is studied. The fourth are working rooms, and the fifth is a room for storing reagents and other materials. All rooms of the laboratory are locked and sealed after work. The department has the posts of senior chemist, chemist and laboratory assistant.

Factors affecting poisoning are divided into two groups. Main causes: the physico-chemical state of the poison, dose and concentration, distribution in the body, chemical purity. Additional causes: rate and routes of entry, cumulation, combined action with other drugs, body weight, nutrition, sex and age. Allergy and a tendency to toxicomania are also taken into account. Poisoning may also occur with several poisons at the same time.

There are regularities between structure and toxicity. Straight-chain hydrocarbon compounds are more toxic than their isomers; cyclic compounds act more strongly than acyclic ones. Introduction of a hydroxyl group into the molecule reduces toxicity; halogen, nitro groups and a double bond increase it. Richardson's rule: in a homologous series toxicity increases with increasing mass. But HCOOH, CH2O and CH3OH are considered stronger poisons than the following members.

Objects of analysis are divided into three groups: objects from the corpse, products and environment, and articles. Objects from the corpse include liver, lungs, brain, blood, urine and vomit. Products and environment include foodstuffs, water, drinks, medicines and air. Articles include clothing, stains, medicine containers and instruments. If the person survives, gastric lavage fluid, vomit, blood and urine are taken; their common name is biological specimen.

The procedure for preserving and dispatching objects. On hot days, a biological specimen sent to a distant place is preserved with ethyl alcohol; a sample of the alcohol is sent together with the preserved specimen. If the specimen must be tested for ethyl alcohol and nitrite, preservation with ethyl alcohol is forbidden. The jar containing the biological specimen is tightly closed and sealed with a wax seal. The label states the surname, first name and year of birth of the deceased and the name of the organ, the number of the forensic medical examination report and the serial number of the jar. A referral from the forensic medical expert or a decision of the investigating authority is sent to the laboratory together with the specimen.

t: Poisons: groups by method of isolation
n: Toxic substances are divided into 6 groups according to the method of isolation. The first is volatile poisons distilled with steam: cyanide, acetic acid, alcohol, aldehyde, phenols, toxic halogen compounds. Barbiturates, alkaloids and nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds are isolated with acidified water or alcohol. Metallic poisons and arsenic are isolated by mineralisation. Mineral acids and alkalis, and salts of alkali metals are isolated by maceration or dialysis; pesticides and cardiac glycosides by an organic solvent. Tetraethyl lead, zinc phosphide and fluorides are determined by special methods.

From powders, tablets, capsules, plant parts and dry extracts, a sample is taken without a fixed quantity. The smallest quantity of the sample must be at the limit determined by the most sensitive methods. Such samples are usually taken in the course of investigative and operational measures and are considered physical evidence. By the requirement of the law, the analytical chemist is obliged to carry out analysis of every separate sample of physical evidence submitted by the court.

The main purpose of sampling is to ensure the reliability and correct performance of chemical analyses. Samples are taken in accordance with the principles of analytical chemistry and the national reference publications based on the pharmacopoeia. Sometimes, for legal reasons, the rules cannot be followed, for example when the physical evidence must be kept as an exhibit. Barbiturate evidence is often in the form of capsules and tablets, which shows that it was illegally diverted from legal trade.

t: Sampling from an object in a single package
n: The simplest way of sampling an object in a single package: when objects are collected in one package, the sample is taken from the package. The sample is placed in a clean plastic bag and its weight is recorded. The simplest way to homogenise powders is to shake the plastic bag thoroughly. If the powder contains granules, they are passed through a fine sieve or ground with a special device.

The ring-cone-quartering method is considered an alternative. The sample is mixed, ground and placed in the shape of a cone on a flat surface. The cone is divided into 4 parts; two opposite quarters are taken and the other two are returned to the bag. If the quantity of the sample needs to be reduced, the ring, cone and quartering are repeated.

t: Urine: the most commonly used specimen
n: The biological specimen most commonly used for the analysis of toxic substances is urine. There are three reasons: urine contains the most information; many poisons and their metabolites are excreted in urine; and taking the sample causes the person no physical discomfort. Additional samples: blood, saliva, hair and nails. In case of death, internal organs are taken, most often the liver.

t: Rules for taking a urine sample
n: Rules for taking a urine sample. The collection of urine and other samples is carried out under the supervision of a legal entity. It is necessary to avoid cases of substitution and the use of specially pre-prepared samples, for example with vinegar or tanning substances. The volume of urine taken for analysis must be not less than 250 ml. If the volume is small, this must be indicated in the record.

t: Checking a urine sample for falsification
n: Checking a urine sample for falsification. To detect the possibility of falsification, the urine sample is immediately subjected to a preliminary inspection. Within 5 minutes of collection, the temperature must be within 32.5-37.7 °C and the pH 5-7. On visual inspection, colour and sediment are assessed; they must be natural. If there is a noticeable difference, a new sample must be taken under stricter supervision.

t: Storing the sample and preparing for dispatch
n: Storing the sample and preparing for dispatch. The sample taken is placed in 2 containers. Names are written on the containers, a code is assigned and they are sealed. Toxic substances are analysed from the sample in one container. The sample in the second container is kept for control analysis.

In analysing urine one must not forget that endogenous and exogenous background substances may be encountered. Endogenous substances include amino acids, sugars, biogenic amines, urea, peptides, steroids and urobilin. Exogenous substances include metabolites of foods and of drugs and poisons, for example metabolites of barbiturates and 1,4-benzodiazepines. That is, background compounds can interfere with the result of the analysis.

Before analysis, urine is treated in various ways. The table gives four methods: evaporation, chromatographic separation, solid sorbent and extraction. Evaporation is carried out directly; chromatographic separation and solid sorbent serve to purify from foreign substances. Among them, liquid-liquid extraction is considered the most widespread method.

t: Practical work: preparing liver for analysis
n: Practical work: preparing liver for analysis. Each student is given 100.0 g of liver and 25.0 ml of urine; the students carry out the preparation with their own hands. First, gloves and a mask are put on. The liver is minced; the consistency and morphological structure of the specimen are examined. Finally, exogenous and endogenous admixtures are checked and preliminary conclusions are given.

t: Appearance of the object: foreign admixtures and odour
n: Let us assess foreign admixtures and odour from the appearance of the object. By eye or under the microscope, admixtures characteristic of a poison may be found in the object: porcelain-like crystals of arsenic oxide, prismatic crystals of strychnine nitrite. A foreign admixture is removed from the object with forceps and tested for the suspected substance. The smell of bitter almonds may point to cyanides, the smell of pyridine bases to denatured alcohol. Odour is well perceived mainly in an object that has not putrefied; in putrefaction, products alter the smell of poisons.

t: Preliminary assessment by colour and pH
n: A preliminary assessment is made by colour and pH. A yellow colour may be characteristic of picric acid, strychnine and chromates, and black of sulphuric acid. The acidity or alkalinity of the medium is determined with various indicators. The pH range of litmus is 5.0-8.0, of Congo red 3.0-5.2, and of phenolphthalein 8.2-10.0.

Let us interpret the pH result. If the pH is 3 or less, it mainly indicates the presence of mineral acids or a large amount of organic acids. A weakly acidic reaction often shows that fermentation has taken place in the organs, especially putrefied ones. An alkaline reaction directs that the object be tested for alkalis or carbonates.

We monitor the purity of reagents with the Marsh reaction. The reaction proceeds in three stages: purity of reagents, detection of arsenic and authenticity of the stain. The Marsh apparatus is assembled and operated for 1 hour. After an hour, no brown-grey stain should form in the cooled part. The absence of a stain shows that the reagents used are pure from the forensic chemical point of view.

Rules for reagent purity. Reagents, vessels and instruments used in the examination must be chemically pure. The purity of a reagent is tested with the method and reaction that are used, in the maximum quantity needed for the analysis. The SOP acceptance criterion: the reagents used and the control sample must not give a positive reaction for the substance being determined, for example mercury.

t: Retention periods for evidence and documents
n: Retention periods for evidence and documents. A preserved specimen is kept for up to 1 year. Documents are kept in a safe and are destroyed after 1 year. Specimens containing alcohol are destroyed after 1 month. The expert chemist is responsible for keeping the physical evidence received from the start of the examination until its end.

Rules for documenting the result. In the description of the appearance of the physical evidence, the full appearance, packaging, container, sealing and inscriptions on the packaging are recorded. The colour, odour, weight and pH of the medium of the physical evidence must also be recorded. In writing the report, giving formulae and the names of authors is forbidden; methods and calculations are written on the basis of the working notebook.

t: What is taken into account in assessing the result
n: What is taken into account in assessing the result? When a substance is detected, quantitative analysis is always carried out, because in some cases reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may occur. Reasons why a poison is not found: elimination from the body before death, metabolism, complete decomposition, binding with another substance and low sensitivity of the method. If the reaction is positive, the substance may have been taken as a medicine, may be naturally present in the object, for example metals, putrefaction products may have given the reaction, or the substance may have been added from the external environment.

No conclusion can be drawn on the basis of the preliminary examination. If the tentative result is positive, the main examination is mandatory. Some tentative methods, although sensitive, are not specific, so the result is confirmed by additional analysis. At the same time, the preliminary examination helps to exclude many poisons or to suggest which poison may be present.

t: The "Why?" technique and the cluster method
n: The "Why?" technique and the cluster method are used in the session. In the "Why?" technique, learners formulate a problem in small groups. A diagram is drawn and the process continues until the primary cause of the problem is found. Then the small groups join together, opinions are compared, brought into a common diagram and the results are presented. The cluster topic: objects and physical evidence brought for forensic chemical analyses.

A brief reminder on ethics and deontology. The activity of a medical worker is based on a high standard of ethics and deontological rules. A medical worker must, despite any pressure, refuse to act contrary to the law and the norms of morality. A medical worker is strictly forbidden to give an incorrect or inaccurate conclusion, as well as all kinds of fraud.

t: Numbers of the session at a glance
n: Let us memorise the numbers of the session at a glance. The volume of urine taken for analysis must be not less than 250 ml. The temperature must be 32.5-37.7 °C and the pH 5-7. The sample taken is placed in 2 containers: one for analysis, the other for control. In the practical work each student is given 100.0 g of liver and 25.0 ml of urine.

Review questions. First: the significance and tasks of the toxicological chemistry module; objects and the requirements for them. Second: examination of the consistency and morphological structure of the object; determining the state of the physical evidence. Third: what requirements are placed on powders, biological fluids and biological specimens? Fourth: preparing objects for analysis.

Conclusion of the session. The types of objects, packaging and integrity, colour, medium, consistency and admixtures were studied. Urine sample: volume not less than 250 ml; temperature 32.5-37.7 °C; pH 5-7; two containers, for analysis and for control. Reagent purity is confirmed by a control test, for example by the absence of a stain in the Marsh apparatus.
